description: I am a software developer based in Edmonton, Canada, with interests in machine learning, astronomy, and space exploration. I enjoy building software that bridges technology and scientific discovery.
summary:
SPHEREx Watch is a browser tool for hunting moving and changing objects in infrared data from NASA SPHEREx, including a possible Planet X. You enter any sky coordinates, and it pulls small image cutouts of that spot from NASA's IRSA archive. It lines every visit up on one sky grid and blinks through them in time order at a single wavelength, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out.
On request, difference imaging takes away the steady sky and finds what changed. 

A lightweight machine-learning model (a gradient-boosted decision tree) then ranks the results and shows which measurements drove each score. The model only suggests: a person accepts or discards every candidate. 

A Gaia DR3 star overlay, shifted for each star's motion, helps rule out known stars. A Spectrum tab measures a source's brightness across all 102 SPHEREx wavelength channels.

This matters because SPHEREx re-images the entire sky every six months, and faint, slow-moving objects like distant planets or nearby brown dwarfs are easy to miss without a human looking. SPHEREx Watch lets anyone help search. Every result records which data products and processing versions it came from, so findings can be traced and repeated. Everything is fetched only when needed and then cached.
details:
SPHEREx Watch

Overview

SPHEREx Watch is a browser-based tool for finding moving and changing objects in NASA SPHEREx infrared data. Users enter sky coordinates (RA/Dec) and a field of view of up to 0.25°. The tool queries NASA's IRSA archive, downloads only relevant image cutouts, and aligns observations onto a shared, north-up sky grid.

Key Features

  • Time-domain exploration: The Time tab blinks through observations at a single wavelength channel and detector, making changes over time easier to identify. Users can pan, zoom, annotate sources and inspect image quality.
  • Astronomical overlays: Gaia DR3 stars are positioned using their measured proper motions at each observation date. Quality masks and per-frame diagnostics help distinguish real sources from artifacts.
  • Candidate detection: On-demand difference imaging PSF-matches and flux-scales observations before comparing each epoch against the median of the others. Signals of 5σ or greater are detected and linked into transients, variables or moving tracks.
  • Explainable ML: A gradient-boosted decision tree ranks candidates and explains which features influenced each score. Human reviewers make every final accept/reject decision.
  • Spectral analysis: The Spectrum tab measures a selected source across all 102 SPHEREx wavelength channels, covering 0.75–5 µm.

Benefits and Intended Impact

SPHEREx re-images the entire sky every six months, creating an opportunity to detect faint, slow-moving objects such as nearby brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets and potentially a distant Planet X.

Automated pipelines can miss unusual objects, while human observers are particularly good at recognizing motion through blinking images. SPHEREx Watch combines both approaches, allowing students, amateur astronomers and researchers to explore real observations and identify candidates for follow-up.

Every result records its data product IDs, release, processing, pipeline and model versions, making discoveries traceable and reproducible. Searches can also be shared through their URL. No installation or specialized hardware is required.

Tools and Technologies

  • Backend: Go, SQLite (WAL mode), pure-Go database driver.
  • Frontend: SvelteKit 2, Svelte 5, Vite and Bun. Custom HTML Canvas and SVG visualizations.
  • Machine Learning: Python, scikit-learn and GradientBoostingClassifier (100 trees, depth 3). The model is trained offline, validated on held-out sky fields, and exported to JSON for inference in Go.
  • Data Sources: NASA IRSA SPHEREx archive and cutout services; Gaia DR3 through IRSA cone search.

Creativity and Innovation

SPHEREx Watch combines astronomical blinking, a technique used by Clyde Tombaugh to discover Pluto in the 1930s, with modern difference imaging and explainable machine learning.

Time-domain and spectral analysis remain separate, allowing users to investigate both an object's movement and its infrared characteristics. Gaia proper-motion corrections provide moving reference points for known stars, helping reduce false positives.

Factors Considered

  • Scientific integrity: Compare matching channels and sky grids without combining detector arrays. Preserve data provenance and require human verification of candidates.
  • Efficiency: Download cutouts on demand, cache results with content-based keys and LRU eviction, deduplicate requests and compute only when needed.
  • Responsible ML: Use a lightweight, interpretable model that does not automatically retrain from user decisions.
  • Accessibility: Provide a browser-based interface that runs on ordinary laptops, with collapsible panels for easier exploration and annotation.
